settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The deny check does exist and does throw JSONException on match (lines 362-367); it is a real guard, not an absent one.

Operators can extend the list at startup via the documented DENY_PROPERTY system property (lines 122-124, 288-291) or programmatically via addDeny (lines 279-286), so the default is not necessarily the deployed configuration.

The JVMs in the read build target 1.5 (pom.xml:28), while some well-known gadget classes (e.g. com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl) appeared in later JDKs, so gadget availability is environment-dependent and not proven here.

Searching the repository for 'AutoType', 'checkAutoType', and 'autoType' returned no matches, so the newer checkAutoType flow is simply not part of this snapshot; there is no allow-list I can point to and claim is bypassed.
candidates.description:
In ParserConfig the blocklist-based guard for type-name-driven deserialization is weak in two ways that are visible in the read source.

(a) Minimal default policy: the class field denyList is initialized to only {"java.lang.Thread"} (line 147). The constructor calls addDeny("java.lang.Thread") (line 263) and addItemsToDeny(DENYS) (line 264), where DENYS is populated from the JVM system property "fastjson.parser.deny" via readSystemDenyPropety() -> IOUtils.getStringProperty(DENY_PROPERTY) (lines 122-124, 288-291). There is no built-in list of dangerous classes (no JDK/JNDI/rowset/gadget entries) in this source. Consequently the effective protection depends entirely on an external system property and, by default, blocks a single class name.

(b) Prefix matching against a normalized name: the deny enforcement in getDeserializer(Class, Type) computes `String className = clazz.getName(); className = className.replace('$', '.');` (lines 360-361) and then, for each deny entry, throws only if `className.startsWith(deny)` (lines 362-367). Because the compared name has '$' replaced by '.', any deny entry that itself contains '$' (e.g. a property-supplied inner-class name) can never match the normalized className, so such entries silently fail to block. Conversely the check remains a raw startsWith prefix test, so it is a name-shape heuristic rather than an authoritative type restriction.

The net effect within the read spans is that the only type-name restriction mechanism present is a short, configuration-fallible prefix blocklist evaluated on a normalized class name, while the class->deserializer selection that follows (lines 442-464, including createJavaBeanDeserializer at 469+) will build a deserializer for any class that is not caught by this list. Whether an attacker-controlled type string can actually reach this guard, and whether a deserializer for a dangerous class is then instantiated, depends on callers outside the read spans (DefaultJSONParser/TypeUtils/JavaBeanDeserializer were not read as source), so this is reported as a candidate weakness in the guard's design, not as a demonstrated vulnerability.
missing_evidence: ParserConfig.java lines 560-706 were not read; any allow-list logic or additional checks after line 559 are unexamined.
DefaultJSONParser.java parseObject '@type' handling was only seen via search excerpts, not read as original source, so runtime reachability of this guard from untrusted input is unconfirmed.
TypeUtils.loadClass, JavaBeanDeserializer, MapDeserializer, MiscCodec, and ThrowableDeserializer were not read, so the exact class-load/instantiation chain and any per-call restrictions are unknown.
No test or configuration shows a concrete default deployment relying only on the built-in denyList.
Whether a class name containing '$' can be supplied as a deny entry through the system property in a way that matters in practice is not demonstrated.
preconditions: Application deserializes untrusted JSON with a ParserConfig whose deny list was not extended (the default state shown in lines 147/263-264).
The JVM does not set -Dfastjson.parser.deny to a comprehensive list (lines 122-124, 288-291).
A caller supplies a type name that the parser path resolves to a Class before getDeserializer(Class,Type) is invoked (caller not read in the allowed spans).
The target class name is not covered by the short denyList prefix entries, or the corresponding deny entry contains '$' and is defeated by the replace('$','.') normalization (lines 360-361).
candidates.title: Type-name deny list in ParserConfig is minimal and its prefix check is applied to the '$'-normalized name, weakening class-name blocklisting
